analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices for the most expensive brand-name drugs and adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage.
analysis.headline: The House passed the drug price negotiation bill 230 to 192, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law forbids the government from negotiating what Medicare pays for prescription drugs. This bill would change that: the government would negotiate maximum prices for the costliest brand-name drugs that face no generic competition — 25 in the first year, growing to 50 — with the price capped at roughly what other wealthy countries pay. It would also penalize manufacturers whose prices rise faster than inflation, cap seniors' yearly drug out-of-pocket costs, add dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare, and fund research and opioid programs with the savings. It passed the House on December 12, 2019, 230-192, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and people with disabilities on Medicare, who would pay less for expensive brand-name drugs and get a hard limit on yearly out-of-pocket drug costs. Low-income Medicare beneficiaries would qualify for more premium and cost-sharing help, and all beneficiaries would gain dental, vision, and hearing coverage. People with private insurance would get the negotiated prices too, unless their insurer opted out. Savings would also accrue to the federal Medicare program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and people with drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: Under current law the government is prohibited from negotiating Medicare drug prices; the bill would require HHS to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and for at least 25 (rising to 50) single-source brand-name drugs that lack generic competition and rank among the costliest nationwide.

The negotiated price could not exceed 120% of the average price in six other wealthy countries (Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, the UK), or 85% of the U.S. list price where international data is unavailable.
Manufacturers would owe rebates to Medicare for covered drugs costing $100 or more whose prices rise faster than inflation, and would face civil penalties for noncompliance.
The bill would lower Medicare's annual out-of-pocket drug spending threshold and eliminate cost-sharing above it, and allow some beneficiaries to spread out their payments.
Medicare would be expanded to cover dental and oral health care, hearing aids and hearing treatment, and eyeglasses and vision services.
Savings would fund NIH and FDA innovation projects, an Opioid Epidemic Response Fund, community health centers, and expanded subsidies for low-income beneficiaries.

Manufacturers that refuse to negotiate face an excise tax on sales that starts at 65% of the sale and escalates to 95%, plus civil monetary penalties of up to ten times the gap between the price charged and the negotiated maximum.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers bear the cost: lower prices on their most profitable single-source drugs, inflation rebates on Medicare sales, price-increase disclosure requirements, and an escalating excise tax (up to 95% of sales) and penalties if they refuse to negotiate. Insurers and pharmacy middlemen also face new reporting and anti-spread-pricing rules in Medicaid.

drawbacks.text: The bill's price caps apply only to the most expensive single-source drugs, and even the cap — 120% of the average foreign price — would still allow prices well above what other wealthy countries pay.

Critics in the House argued that price negotiation could reduce the development of new drugs; Rep. Upton's motion to recommit would have delayed the bill's effective date until HHS certified that implementation was not projected to result in fewer new drug applications for unmet medical needs and life-saving cures. The motion failed 196-226.
Private insurers may simply opt out of the negotiated prices, and plans that opt out must be publicly listed, limiting how far the savings extend beyond Medicare.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who take expensive brand-name drugs, the gains are direct and large: lower prices, a hard cap on yearly out-of-pocket costs, and new Medicare dental, vision, and hearing benefits. The cost falls almost entirely on an industry whose U.S. prices for these drugs run far above what the same drugs cost in other developed countries. The genuine trade-off is innovation: tighter prices on the biggest-selling drugs could shrink the revenue that funds research on new medicines. The bill tries to limit that by targeting only drugs without generic competition and by funding NIH and FDA research with the savings, but the concern is legitimate and was the core argument against it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 230-192 on December 12, 2019, but the Senate never voted on it — it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced September 19, 2019, and referred to three committees; the Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported 30-22, and Ways and Means and Education and Labor also reported it in December.
On December 12, 2019, the House defeated a motion to recommit (a Republican-led change to delay the bill's effective date) by 196-226, then passed the bill 230-192.
The House vote split almost entirely by party: 228 of 229 Democrats voted yes and only 2 of 193 Republicans did.

The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar in September 2020 — but never debated or voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers came out ahead: their prices on the most profitable single-source drugs stay un-negotiated, the inflation rebates never took effect, and the escalating excise tax and penalties never applied. The Senate chamber that never voted set the outcome.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: House Energy and Commerce Committee Chairman; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and led it through committee, which ordered it reported 30-22.

for.name: House Democratic caucus
for.what_they_did: Gave the bill all 228 of its yes votes — every voting Democrat supported it — and brought it to the floor under a rule with four hours of debate.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from September 2020 until the Congress ended.

against.name: 191 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage 191-2, and offered a motion to recommit that would have delayed the bill until HHS certified it would not reduce development of new drugs.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Drug manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a large-scale campaign against the bill, arguing government price-setting would reduce investment in new medicines.

sides.party_line_note: The House passage vote was almost perfectly partisan: 228 of 229 voting Democrats voted yes, while only 2 of 193 Republicans did; the Senate, then controlled by Republicans, never voted.
